name: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
aliases: primary cutaneous CD30+ anaplastic large-cell lymphoma

clinicalPearls: Presents typically as a solitary or localised, often ulcerating, skin nodule or tumour in an older adult, without evidence of systemic lymphoma at diagnosis
Part of the primary cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative spectrum, sharing a border with lymphomatoid papulosis
By definition, more than three-quarters of the large tumour cells express CD30
Unlike systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, the cutaneous form is usually ALK-negative and lacks the associated ALK translocation, and follows a much more indolent course
Lesions may partially regress spontaneously, and multifocal skin disease can occur without implying systemic involvement
Staging is essential to exclude systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma secondarily involving the skin, which carries a different prognosis and treatment
Localised disease is often managed with radiotherapy or surgical excision, reserving systemic therapy for extensive or extracutaneous disease
reference.pathophysiology: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma is a T-cell neoplasm composed of large cells with anaplastic, pleomorphic, or immunoblastic morphology, the majority strongly expressing the CD30 activation antigen. It arises within and is largely confined to the skin, and in contrast to systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma it usually lacks ALK gene rearrangement. The tumour sits at the aggressive end of the cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative spectrum yet behaves indolently, with a tendency to remain localised and occasionally to regress, reflecting relative immune containment. Regional lymph node spread can occur but distant dissemination is uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma with cutaneous involvement
Other CD30-positive T-cell lymphomas in the skin
Poorly differentiated carcinoma or melanoma mimicking a skin tumour
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry demonstrating CD30 positivity in the majority of large cells
ALK immunostaining and, where indicated, testing for ALK rearrangement
Staging imaging (CT or PET-CT) to exclude systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
Bone marrow examination when systemic disease is suspected
Clinicopathological correlation to separate from lymphomatoid papulosis
redFlags: Extracutaneous or nodal disease indicating possible systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
Rapidly progressive or widely disseminated lesions
Systemic B-symptoms suggesting more aggressive disease
Failure of a presumed benign lesion to regress, prompting biopsy and staging
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally very good with high survival for skin-limited disease, though extensive multifocal cutaneous disease, leg involvement, or extracutaneous spread can worsen outcome.
pitfalls: Failing to stage and thereby missing systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma involving the skin
Confusing the entity with lymphomatoid papulosis without clinicopathological correlation
Overtreating indolent, localised disease with aggressive systemic chemotherapy
Assuming ALK positivity, which is characteristic of systemic rather than primary cutaneous disease
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Confirm the diagnosis with careful staging to exclude systemic (nodal or extracutaneous) involvement before classifying disease as primary cutaneous.
For a solitary or localized lesion, treat with surgical excision and/or local radiotherapy, with dose and fractionation set by the treating radiation oncologist.
Consider a period of observation for an asymptomatic, regressing lesion, since lesions can regress spontaneously.
For recurrent skin-limited disease, consider oral methotrexate or other cytotoxic agents.
Recognize that multifocal skin disease at presentation does not by itself indicate systemic disease, but warrants the same staging workup as solitary disease.
For relapsed or refractory disease, or disease progressing after radiotherapy or at least one systemic therapy, consider brentuximab vedotin, a CD30-directed antibody-drug conjugate.
Monitor patients on brentuximab vedotin for peripheral neuropathy, the most common adverse effect, which is usually reversible.

Reserve multi-agent cytotoxic chemotherapy for patients refractory to more targeted approaches or needing rapid palliation of extensive disease, given substantial myelosuppression and infection risk with limited durability of response.
Consider nucleoside analogs or gemcitabine as single agents for refractory systemic-type presentations, with prophylactic antimicrobial and antiviral coverage during nucleoside analog therapy.
Distinguish from systemic ALK-positive ALCL by absence of ALK translocation and absence of epithelial membrane antigen expression.

Maintain ongoing dermatologic surveillance given overlap with lymphomatoid papulosis and the risk of another lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, ALCL, or Hodgkin lymphoma) preceding or following presentation.
Follow patients after treatment for local recurrence, new cutaneous lesions, and signs of systemic spread, with surveillance cadence guided by institutional or NCCN cutaneous lymphoma practice.
Refer to a dermatology or cutaneous-lymphoma specialist center at diagnosis for staging and management.
Refer to radiation oncology when local radiotherapy is being considered, and to hematology-oncology for evaluation of systemic therapy in recurrent, multifocal, or refractory disease.
